purpose: Prazosin is mainly used to treat high blood pressure (hypertension). It is also sometimes prescribed to help with nightmares and sleep problems related to PTSD (post-traumatic stress disorder). In some cases, doctors use it to help men with an enlarged prostate urinate more easily.
how_it_works: Your body has tiny receptors in your blood vessels called alpha-1 receptors. Prazosin blocks these receptors, which causes your blood vessels to relax and widen. When your blood vessels open up, your heart doesn't have to work as hard, and your blood pressure goes down.
common_side_effects: Dizziness or lightheadedness, especially when you stand up quickly. Headache, feeling tired or drowsy, nausea, and a stuffy or runny nose are also fairly common. These effects are usually mild and often improve as your body gets used to the medication.
warnings: The biggest concern with prazosin is something called 'first-dose syncope,' which means you could faint or feel very dizzy after your very first dose or after a dose increase. Always take your first dose at bedtime to reduce this risk. Do not drive or do anything dangerous until you know how this medicine affects you. Tell your doctor if you feel faint or have chest pain. Do not stop taking it suddenly without talking to your doctor first.
typical_dosing: Most people start with a very low dose of 1 mg taken at bedtime to reduce the risk of dizziness. Your doctor may slowly increase your dose over time, typically ranging from 1 mg to 20 mg per day, divided into two or three doses. Always follow your doctor's specific instructions for your dose.
